utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, are you ready to resume the cross-examination of Mr. Hermer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I am. Although you know that normally you remind the witness that he is still under oath, under solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I intended to do, but thank you for assisting me. May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you made yesterday? It might be unnecessary, but I would still like to remind you. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, another thing I very often do is to indicate how much time the examination in chief has taken. It is one hour and 42 minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will continue my cross-examination in French and I will also listen on both channels so that I can have everything we need. Here we are. Witness, I am going to ask you to answer as briefly as possible because everyone here would like to save as much time as possible. So if I am interrupting you during your answer, it is not because I am being rude, but because -- in order to save time. I am sure you will understand. Witness, in relation to your testimony yesterday on page 33, you spoke of some agreements that the parties reached in relation to Mount Igman. Could you, in a few words, tell us what was that about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The agreement was reached, was brokered, if you like, by UNPROFOR, and was designed to bring about some resolution over the area of ground known as Mount Igman. The agreement, as I understood it, was to allow a United Nations force to stay permanently and police the Igman area, thus preventing that area being fully controlled by either side in the conflict, and thus hopefully preventing further conflicts in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If we are talking about kind of security corridor; is that what the idea was behind it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A security corridor would be one way of describing it. That would be apt, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I will come back to it. I would like to go into another line of questioning now. We have testimony, Major, that is saying quite often that there was -- there were weapons, mobile artillery weapons, artillery means in Sarajevo. For instance, there was small lorries or trucks which were used to transport mortars or even private vehicles that were used for this purpose. Have you, with your own eyes, seen such means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what you saw, briefly, and when and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My experience of such things, I could not put a specific date on that, I am afraid. These experiences occurred throughout my time. The kind of things which I witnessed personally, to which I believe you are alluding, were vehicles such as civilian cars, for example, Volkswagens, that would have improvised weapon systems in the vehicles. The vehicles would be significantly modified to allow this to take place. I saw what would essentially be considered to be civilian, rather than military, trucks being used to transport weapons of a light nature, be it small mortars or medium mortars. And also one vehicle which was prominent in Sarajevo was what I would term a "flat bed" or flat back" lorry on which was mounted heavy machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And very briefly, what kind of machine-gun, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A heavy machine-gun, 12.7 calibre or larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. You spoke earlier of several vehicles, civilian vehicles, that were modified in order to make them into military vehicles. Could you tell us something about their number, how many units would that be? How many vehicles, rather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can recall in terms of civilian vehicles, family saloon car, for example, probably seeing personally two or three of these vehicles which had been modified with armour, plating, windows removed and weapons attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I am not going on to another line of questioning and this is in relation to the answers that you have already given. You said, Witness, that you were in contact with the HQ in Lukavica with an ordinary civilian telephone line. Could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you confirm, if this was the case, that the military parties that were present and confronting each other in Sarajevo, were they able to use those civilian telephone lines for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no personal knowledge of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Now, sir, yesterday you said that you briefly saw on two occasions General Galic, page 49 line 5. Could you confirm that in fact you never discussed with him directly on any subject matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As my memory serves me, no, I never had any detailed discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your answer. You also said, 48.20, that the offices of Major Indjic, who later became colonel, were on the first floor; is that what you can confirm for us now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I said the first floor, I meant the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Sir, you said in relation to Major Indjic that he was working for the Sarajevo Romanija headquarters. What are the factual elements that would help you to assume -- not to assume this, but to know this, as a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I remember from yesterday, that was, in fact, an assumption, based on my experience and the way in which Major Indjic was introduced to me at the outset of our working relationship.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you are confirming that this is just an interpretation on your part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, on several occasions, on page 40, line 21, you said that when there were shots that were being fired onto the city, there were apparently no military targets that were targeted. You said: "There was no military target present." That is a quote. Sir, my question is the following: In relation to what you said, could you categorically exclude that on the locations that you were referring to, there were no mobile targets like the ones that you just described for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. So if I understand you correctly, there is a possibility, a theoretical possibility, that there were or there was a mobile military target at a location that you described as being a civilian target or a civilian location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Yesterday, asked by our learned colleagues by the Prosecution, you said that the incident reports on outgoing and incoming were about 1 to 100. On which base -- on what are you basing this, this percentage, this relation, this ratio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ratio is a pure numerical one based on the number of incident reports relating specifically to impacts in the city versus impacts outside the city, incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And to ask you another question, did you yourself, on the basis of the Sit-Reps or Inc-Reps, did you ever make that calculation of a ratio? Have you ever done such calculation yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you indicate to us on the basis of which, which period and which report exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not give you a specific report, but the calculation was something which I was doing regularly for use in briefings within the PTT building. I never, to my knowledge, formally articulated that on paper or reported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I am going to interrupt you. Thank you for your answer. But I remember that what you said last time - that is yesterday - that it was a report about 1 to 2 per cent. Is that what you remember as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be the ratio I would conclude after doing my mental calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am going to come back to another point now. The incident that you referred to in the area of Holiday Inn, do you remember the moment during the examination of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, first of all, you said in relation to the shots that you were able to see on the facade of a building, that there were some flashes. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You also said that on the basis of your experience and of your knowledge of the field and the maps that you made, you were able to locate almost with certainty that the shots were coming from a building which was under Serb control. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Since you did it on the basis of maps, what was the street where this building was located, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the name of the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your answer. Sir, I asked you yesterday about your training and your military qualifications, and you answered and I thank you for it. Now, sir, would you agree with me if you considered that the physical location where the supreme commander of an army is, in the time of war, a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your "definitely." Now, is it true that the Presidency was such a location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand it, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, sir. Sir, what is the distance between the Holiday Inn and the Presidency building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From memory, I would say in the region of 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the Presidency building is located almost opposite the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not almost opposite, no. Close to, but not almost opposite, in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you think that this distance was a lot shorter than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Fine. Sir, do you know that strategic meetings were taking place on the day of the incident -- incident in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, do you know that on the day of the incident, there were combats or combat activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] In and around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, in relation to your answer, could you categorically exclude the possibility that troop movement were about to intervene or were intervening at that moment in the area of those shots, and at the time, you didn't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can categorically say that, in the area of those shots, there was no military activity happening or about to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How could you, sir, exclude this possibility if you did not know that a meeting was going to take place in these buildings, a strategic meeting, if certain military personnel, in uniforms or not, were supposed to be there at that time, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The subject of the fire, as we discussed yesterday, was not military. There was no indication --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now I am going to interrupt you. Could you please answer my question? My question was the following: How could you exclude the possibility of what I have just indicated to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You also said, and this is page 59, line 1 and the following one, you said that a little before this incident, as far as you know, there was no military target in that area. How can you be so sure of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on the investigations of the -- my colleagues who were there on the scene shortly after it had commenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, do you know and -- do you know, sir, if in the area of the Holiday Inn there was -- there were some elements that belonged to elite units of the Muslim army, that is, the snipers, and that they were about to regroup?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you said earlier that you were not able to know where the mobile military targets were like the ones you spoke about. Could you exclude the possibility that at the time of the incident, just before it, that there was precisely such a mobile military target in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. You spoke of sniper alley, or what was called the sniper alley, and you said that it was located along government buildings. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. These government buildings, do you also mean the Presidency by those buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That is, practically, theoretically, militarily, that was the residency of the supreme commander of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, as far as you know, and in your capacity as a professional soldier that you are, could you confirm that this is the case: That this location of the Presidency was frequently used for meetings between military personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, a technical question also and I am going to call on your experience here. You spoke yesterday about very young people who were armed and below the age of 16, and that they were bearing rifles, bearing arms. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I used the expression "bearing arms" yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I think this was my expression, but you were talking about very young people who were very near military situations and military locations. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All right. What I will go back to that question a bit later. Now, as far as the armed people are concerned, can you confirm for us -- you can't hear me? [In English] I can't do anything for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I can't hear the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English booth now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only just.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear it now? Is it better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear it but not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. It is adequate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I will listen for a while to the English booth in order to see whether the sound quality is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I apologise for this, but let us go back to what we had been talking before. Can you please tell me, based on your experience, how many armed people were there in the town of Sarajevo? I mean, the Muslim army here, the so-called Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a bit difficult to answer that question simply because there were more men able to bear weapons than there were weapons in existence. The figure, as I remember, that we were working to as a broad figure was that approximately 10.000 men could bear arms in the city at any one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say, "10.000 men able to bear arms" you most probably believe that those people were armed at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I believe is that there was the ability to -- for 10.000 men to carry arms simultaneously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, let me tell you that according to some figures, there were about 50.000 people who were considered to be soldiers, albeit there were fewer weapons, individual weapons, that could have been distributed to them. Would this figure be acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no means of verifying that, but based upon the number of men I witnessed of soldiering age, I would say that would be a reasonable figure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for this answer. I will go to my next question, sir. Can you please tell us briefly, were there any women in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In active service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of numerical values for those units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you mean do I know how many women were serving, the answer is no, but the ratio of men to women was very small, or rather women to men. It was a very small percentage of females that appeared to be serving.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for this answer, sir. I would go back to some of the things you mentioned during your testimony specifically concerning the firing from DSA, AAA; I mean the anti-aircraft fire artillery. You have told us that these weapons were used in such a way as to -- to be used in the ground mode. Can you confirm that very frequently these were direct hits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, direct hits, do you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] I mean we use it in the direct way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Thanks. [Interpretation] Can you then tell us, please, or can you confirm for us, when this ammunition from the anti-aircraft artillery is used in the direct way, that it practically cannot be used with the detonator or ignition system which has to do with the height of the rocket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That -- as I understand it, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, sir. Now, I will go back to another element of your testimony. We will now turn to one of your lunches, meals, at the PTT building when you were able to witness the attack on the Zuc Mount. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, can you please confirm by saying "yes" or "no" that you watched only that area and that you only saw the area of the impact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. But you can't tell us anything regarding the range of that shot? You can't tell us anything about the distance where this shot originated? Here I am interested in your personal observation, not in the reports that you might have read about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, sir, I have a technical question regarding your training, your education. Can you tell us, when we speak about a distance of 1 vertical kilometre -- I am sorry, horizontal distance, can you tell us what is 10 degrees? What is it in practical terms, what height are we talking about, about 10-degree elevation? I am afraid you did not understand my question. Shall I repeat it for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I understand. My difficulty here is that in the British forces we do not work in degrees, we work in mils.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you approximate? Can you make this conversion and switch from degrees to mils? Sir, if I tell you that if we are speaking about vertical elevations, that is approximately 250 metres, would that seem right to you, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working on about 200, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you. So we are speaking about the same subject. Thank you for your reply. Now, sir, I have the following question: Can you tell us whether the UN forces, whose member you were, adjusted their watches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean synchronized?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That is exactly what I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday, you stated that you were sure about the origin of firing because there was a matter of one or two seconds at the time. However, you can't be certain that your watches showed identical time. Can you be certain of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But in order for everything to be clear, when you say, "that is correct," that means, no, you are not sure, you cannot be sure about that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot be sure that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can you be certain, sir -- so my question is: Can you be certain, can you categorically confirm that in that attack which you witnessed, there was no troop movement, be it the advancement of troops or retreat, with respect to a certain combat line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot state categorically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I will continue with this line of questioning. Sir, you will agree with me if I say that we cannot exclude either an error in elevation or any military target for which you might not know, might not have known at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we cannot exclude that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I will switch to another topic. I just have to check what the time is since the Chamber is very sensitive to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can you tell us how much time we have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When starting this afternoon, you used 37 minutes. I have to add the time. That is from -- let me just have a look, 14.50 until -- it is 14 minutes. You used 77 minutes at this moment, that is one hour and 17 minutes, as far as I can see, and there would be a remainder of 25 minutes. So there would be 25 minutes left. But you know you don't have to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I try to do my best, sir. [Interpretation] Shall I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing, regarding the time schedule. Can you tell us when do you envision for us to have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is appropriate to have the break shortly after 4.00, so that is after you concluded the cross-examination which I expect you to conclude within some 25 minutes, that is 5 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not disappoint you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, let us continue with my questions for you. Thank you for your previous answer. Can you tell me, does the word "oxygen" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand what oxygen is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Does the term "Operation Oxygen" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, have you never heard of an operation which we called here "Operation Oxygen" during which the oxygen bottles were allegedly filled with gunpowder and apparently transported by the members of an UN organisation, and apparently transported to a hospital in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard it as a sort of apocryphal story, but I've never heard it referred to as "Operation Oxygen," no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All right. Now let us forget about this term. But can you tell me, when did you hear of this operation and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot specifically remember when I first encountered this story. It is something which you could say has gone down in UN folklore and is often recounted. I've heard it recounted a number of times, or something similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you heard that from other high ranking officers; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure I heard the story in a bar, and I normally drink with officers of my own rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever heard stories about the same kind of an operation that was called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: "Container."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: "Operation Containers."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not heard of an operation referred to by that name. If you were to elaborate, I might know more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, you will probably ascribe it to the UN folklore once again. However, this was an operation in which allegedly trucks were modified in order to be able to conduct a more or less clandestine transport of weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say I have specifically heard of that incident, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, your response surprises me. You told me that you did not hear specifically of it, but did you hear anything relating to this type of incident, to a similar type of event or something like this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to explain that during my time in Sarajevo, there were many stories like this which were in the public domain. Both sides were -- warring factions, would recount such tales, as would unreliable sources within the UN, and I have since heard other similar stories, but I have no personal experience of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now I will turn to another line of questions. We will go back to the Mount Igman once again. Do you know whether at one point the forces of General Seferovic were able to pass through what we used to call security corridor just a while ago, in order to engage in military operations on the other side of Mount Igman and consequently commit certain crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With regard to the first part of your question, my answer is that logically and the evidence pointed to the fact that there was indeed crossing of this area as certain personalities would appear, both outside and inside Sarajevo, outside beyond the UN safe corridor, which would suggest strongly that there had been some transgression of that area. With regard to the last part, I cannot say whether they were consequently able to commit certain crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, mea culpa. I think I misstated the name. I meant Mr. Sefer Halilovic, that is the person I meant, and does this change your answer in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't change my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we will remain on the same topic. Do you know of a tunnel between Dobrinja and Butmir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us, sir, that this tunnel was equally used for transporting ammunition and weapons into the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot personally confirm that, although it would seem likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, do you know, sir, whether prisoners, maybe prisoner of war, Serb POWs, were used for digging this tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness. You spoke to us about your knowledge of the city of Sarajevo. And could you now tell us where the following places are: The Main Staff of MUP or the MUP command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember the location of that headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, sir, where the 101st, 102nd, and 105th brigades or, rather, their commands were located? Precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, now, I am not asking these questions -- I am not referring only to brigades, but to battalions as well, but if you do not know where the brigades were, then I suppose you don't know where the commands of battalions or lower units were either. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information I was receiving as the operations officer and the MIO, was, if you like, paper information. The observation post staff were the men who would daily visit these locations and knew specifically where they were. So, without a map, it would be more difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am speaking of your personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the other hand, when for example, a shell falls, a random one, how can you categorically, definitely, exclude the possibility that this shell was intended for a very particular specific military target which was maybe located in a residential building, however, in a building where there was a command or headquarters or some kind of a military target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is impossible to categorically definitely exclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Witness, I would like to go back to some other topics. I will -- let me address the registrar and Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to give to the witness document D108, which was used before, and I think that all of us have it. We will use this document in a little bit. And now I would like to focus on some general questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you answered to one of my questions yesterday by saying that you also had some history training, theoretical training, during your education; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We, all of us, know what trench warfare is. Please correct me if I'm mistaken, but please tell me, is it true that this type of warfare was led between 1915 and 1917 before the Brest Litovsk agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are referring to the First World War, the conflict between allies in Germany, then yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It was the only possible reference, isn't it? Now, tell me, sir, regarding this type of warfare, is it true that two armies dug in there and refrained from advancement or trying to conquer new territories? Now I am referring to the front in northern France, practically in Belgium.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I don't understand the question you are asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We are referring to the bois des dames. Is it true in this type of situation, the French army specifically and the German army, were dug in, in the trenches, and there were observing each other, they were shelling each other, but there were not attempting to gain terrain, to gain ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was certainly a classic war of attrition but, ultimately, the aim was to gain ground, yes. The physical circumstances made that very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, practically speaking, these two armies, for two years were shelling each other without gaining any ground, consequently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were minor gains and losses, but in general terms, no, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, if we follow this hypothesis, the shooting from these mined trenches, from trench to trench, this was something that was perfectly acceptable in the art of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When there are purely combatants involved, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer, Witness. Sir, I would like to go back to some other historical questions. As a British officer, I am sure you will be able to answer. 1913, 14, 15, February, 1945, does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1913, 1914, and 1915 and February 1945, are they the dates we are --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No. It is the 13th, the 14th and 15th of February.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. 1945

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps my history is escaping me. We were well into the Allied advance through Europe at that time, approaching the Rhine, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Okay, and Bomber Harris?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. Yes, the dam busters, Bomber Harris and the Allied daylight bombing raids on Germany and the German industrial power base.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you are talking about industrial power, you are talking about the city of Dresden, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dresden in particular is an example which is used to identify that period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And the campaign of the 13th, 14th, and 15th of February, 1945, he was targeting specifically Dresden, do you know how many victims there were, how many casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how many, but I know it was a significant number of civilians that were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it true that we are talking about hundreds of thousands of people who died, burned alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly many thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And for the first time in history, what was used was a huge use of inflammable bombs, incendiary bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is incorrect. They were used primarily on London in 1941, prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I said in such -- on such a vast scale, but that doesn't change the question. There were incendiary bombs that were used, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The question is important. I have to ask you. Historians normally say that there were no large military important targets in Dresden. Now, could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've been giving my learned colleague a bit of leeway here but I am wondering if we have perhaps crossed into the realm of irrelevance at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute? I remember, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that earlier you have asked similar questions to witnesses, and I am not going to disclose to this witness what one of your last questions was, but is there any dispute about it before --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know whether the debate is the correct term to use or "dispute," sorry. But I am trying to find out, this is what happened few years ago and this is just to bring it to the witness that there was a moral condemnation of the fact or perhaps bring it to recognise this, and I believe that this is very important and it is relevant for the case that interests us, and that is Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is that in dispute between the parties? I mean, the rather personal -- I take it it is just one or two more questions and it is your time. We are three minutes off from the time limit. So if you want to use it that way, I don't know whether it is in dispute, Mr. Mundis, whether this has led to any Prosecution, that is -- I didn't want to disclose one of the questions to come, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Certainly not in dispute, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you want to use your remaining time this way, I will even give you the one minute extra that I just took.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed. I am just going to confer for a brief while.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I apologise, sir. I am going to come back to what I was saying. Since I have one minute extra, I am going to try not to use it. Now, sir, could you tell us, as far as you know, as an officer and a man of honour, if any measure was ever taken by anyone who may have taken part or ordered -- taken against anyone who may have taken or ordered these bombardments of Dresden? Was anything ever taken against these people who did that to Dresden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A combination of reasons, I understand. One, in that it helped to secure an Allied victory, which gave it legitimacy as an act, and secondly, that as a collective target, albeit, a civilian target, it was seen as a legitimate means to justify an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I presume the end justified the means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Hermer, I would like to return to the issue that arose immediately prior to the recess last evening and, namely, the use of or the fact that you saw young people close to the front lines. Yesterday, you indicated that you saw young people around military positions. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what specific military positions or what -- or at what locations these military positions were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Young people around military positions was a common feature of that conflict on both sides of the front line. We could be here all day if I give you a list of areas where it occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that it was widespread on both sides of the lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall specifically on how many occasions or approximately how many occasions you saw children with weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Holding weapons or bearing arms?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's start with holding weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Infrequently. A few times, between 5 and 10 times, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And bearing arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never. I never witnessed children bearing arms in a military fashion. Young teenagers, yes, but children, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "bearing arms in a military fashion"? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means that -- by that I am implying that an individual would have ownership of a weapon and would be prepared to use it in an offensive or defensive manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what types of weapons you saw young people carrying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, small arms, rifles, assault rifles, Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what you saw these children or young people doing with these weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Playing or cleaning the weapons. Playing with or cleaning the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on what you saw, are you able to say whether the weapons were the young people's weapons or did they belong to someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In all instances, I am fairly certain that these weapons did not belong to these children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see children around military positions during times when there was active combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time, do you recall whether any of these young people were actually carrying weapons at the time of that combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, my recollection of young people with weapons was invariably when there was a quiet period and administration and relaxation was being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear or receive reports of children becoming casualties by being close to military positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but you also have to consider that many military positions were close to areas inhabited by children, on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you provide any specific examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say certainly the areas of Dobrinja and the southern area of the front line from Lukavica along towards Grbavica. Those areas were heavily inhabited and also extensively fought over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving or hearing about reports of children becoming casualties while carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I am going to move on to a subject that was brought up today and mainly that being, as you have described it, "mobile military targets." Do you recall or do you have any approximate idea as to the number of these mobile military targets, as you have described them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, do you mean across the conflict or in one specific area?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's focus on inside the city of Sarajevo during the five months that you were in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how many, as I think I said earlier. I saw two or three of these type of vehicles personally and I have reports of others, so you have to bear in mind that there were a few vehicles running in the city at that time, due to a lack of fuel. Those which were may well have been used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the five months that you were posted and quartered in the PTT building, how frequently would you be out on the streets of Sarajevo, either travelling from OP to OP or otherwise out on the streets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as possible, daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during this five-month period, you only witnessed mobile military targets on two or three occasions, you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Hermer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that on a number of occasions, there were shells landing close to the OP sites. My understanding is that the OP sites were close to the military sites, to, well, gun sites or something like that. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In most instances, they were fairly near to either the confrontation line or military installations, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you, if you could tell me, when you spoke yesterday of complaints that you presented to Major Indjic, you spoke of some complaints that were to do with shooting that was targeting the UNPROFOR. Did you have an occasion to tell him about the shooting that was targeting civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I understand correctly, you said that at least as far as the sniping activities were concerned, that following your complaints, the shooting stopped, or at least in as far as the incidents -- the incident that you mentioned, when you -- when you -- oh, yes, when you mentioned the CNN, and you said that when you mentioned the CNN who were coming to photograph the site, that the shooting stopped. Now, as far as civilian targets were concerned, did your complaint had any consequences? Did the shooting on civilian targets stop or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there was an acceptance at the outset of the telephone call that something was happening and if there was an agreement reached, that the liaison officer would try to do something and generally that shooting would cease, either naturally or by intervention. It is difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the fact that you mentioned a civilian target, did it influence in any way the decision that was taken, in your opinion? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. On occasions, it was not accepted that the target was civilian, although that was our interpretation. As I said, if there was acceptance, then the answer is yes, there would be an effect and it would stop, generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, this happened that there was an acceptance that civilian targets were targeted or even hit, in any case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That certainly appeared to be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now two brief questions, please. You spoke about -- you spoke about ladies who were bearing arms, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a sense that there were not enough weapons to go around for people who were of military age, so I am a little hesitant to find out was this a phenomenon, were these specific individual cases sporadic, or was this something quite normal and usual, that ladies, as well as young people, were bearing weapons and took part in the combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not commonplace to see women bearing arms. They were an exception and notable as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was an exception that attracted your attention, therefore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So when they are talking about young people, children, you said you saw them playing, and your expression was "playing with weapons." What do you mean by "playing with weapons"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a similar manner that most young boys will play with toy guns, play battles and the like, I witnessed young children at child's play, but using real weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we imagine that these were weapons that were -- could not be used, that they were not actually real weapons, that they had lost their ability to be weapons, their capacity? Or were these weapons that actually could be used for firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would seem extremely unlikely to me that these were what we might call "deactivated weapons". To me, they looked authentic, and considering the environment and the conditions of these weapons, it seems very likely that they were fully active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, when you are talking about cars that were modified to be used for military purpose, did these vehicles bear any kind of insignia which distinguished them from ordinary civilian vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is yes. Generally, they were painted in a military or paramilitary fashion. Some attempt of camouflage may well have been made on the surface of the vehicle. Often, there would be slogans, words or insignia painted on these vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hermer, I also have a few questions for you. You have told us yesterday that on the basis of crater analysis, the range and direction of the firing points could be established. We heard a lot of testimony in this court about direction. Could you please tell us a bit more about how you could establish the range by crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The range assessment doing crater analysis is one of the more difficult elements to assess because there are a number of factors which can make the assessment inaccurate, for example, the height at which the weapon was fired. The height the weapon was fired and the type of charge that was used to fire the weapon will affect the angle of trajectory of the round which makes the impact on the ground distinctive. So, generally, the first thing to do is to assess whether the impact is mortar round or an artillery round, and that is done by looking at the characteristic shape of the impact on the ground. The two are very different. If the ground is very soft, this can be almost impossible to do. Once you have established whether the round was fired by mortar or artillery, the next thing to do is to try to find some trace or remainder of the fuse of the weapon, which would give you an approximate angle of trajectory, be it high angle or low angle. Based upon the size of the impact and any parts that remain of the shell, you can then determine approximately the calibre of the weapon that was used, and by combining all those factors, you can make a deduction with regards to the range of the weapon. The easiest thing to assess is the direction from which the weapon was fired. The pattern on the ground is very distinctive, but the range is much more difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About the charge, what would you know about the charge? Because it is my understanding that it is not one of the least important elements to establish the range.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, with artillery pieces, you are working with fixed shells and fixed charge, but when you are working with mortars, you can vary the amount of charge which is that which fires the round out of the barrel of the weapon. By varying that, you can of course increase the range or decrease the range, and that is used in conjunction with the angle of trajectory of the weapon. So, for example, you might need to use a very high charge and a very high angle of trajectory to achieve a very short range if you have a high feature which you need to clear, for example, a hill. On the other hand, you could use a low angle of trajectory and a low charge to achieve a greater range. And these are the elements which make crater analysis difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand you well that as far as the direction is concerned, that it is far better possible to give firm conclusions if you would compare it with the range?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have another question for you. You told us -- although the transcript says really time was used, but I think you were talking about real time using for establishing gunlines or gun positions. Could you explain to me - gunlines, I think I do understand - but how real time would be used to establish compositions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The time of flight of a round from the point of fire to the point of impact is a very important tool for soldiers to use. By accurately timing that time of flight and taking into account some other variables, it can help you to determine the range at which the weapon was fired. But as I have said, there are other variables such as altitude, the firing point, and any obstacles which need to be cleared which can increase time of flight, but not necessarily range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hermer, my last question to you is: You told us yesterday about the obstruction you experienced when you wanted to move on the Lima side. Did you experience similar obstructions to move on the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such restrictions were occasionally placed upon us, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would compare the obstruction on the Lima side and the Papa side, would you say it was more intense on one of both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gaining clearance to move around the Lima side was generally beset with problems and frequently, without warning, our military observers were confined to their locations. On the Papa side, this was less so, and Bosnian army and government elements were generally happy with us having freedom of movement within the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hermer. This concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for -- well --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...there might be questions. Are they related to any questions of the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe so, Mr. President. I would just like to confer for a couple of seconds because after the questions by the Chamber, General Galic would like to ask some questions, and maybe we can do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...I think it is better to have the break now. We have a shorter time in total so let's have a break of 25 minutes. We resume then at -- if the interpreters would agree with that as an exception, we have a break of 25 minutes, so we start at a quarter to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. General Galic and the Defence of General Galic are grateful for the Chamber for giving us an opportunity to reply to something mentioned by Judge El Mahdi that has to do with women members of the army. General Galic reminded of me an existence of a document and my question is as follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, did you know about a fact that in the 102nd Motorised Brigade of the Muslim army, in which there were some 3500 soldiers, there were at least 236 - the exact number is 236 - women, 7 per cent of which were in command posts, whereas the others were deployed on the front or in combat. Did you know of this? Sir, we are now referring to the 102nd Motorised Brigade. I am now referring to a document in our possession. It is a document dated December 20, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that I specifically remember having been made aware of those figures. They are not -- they don't strike a cord. I can't say I knew that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Didn't you know that there was a significant number of women reservists who were in the 102nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may answer the question, Mr. Hermer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to say that I wasn't aware that the number was -- or the percentage was as high as that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second question was whether you knew that there was a significant number of women reservists. That is not a percentage any more. That was in the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. No I did not know there were a significant number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And still within the same line of questions, do you know, sir, about a document which pertains to demobilisation of children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of any document pertaining to that subject matter, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I take it that there are no further questions, this - and I say now for the second time, Mr. Hermer - concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming and answering questions of all the parties and the Bench. That is important for us to hear witnesses who can tell us about events at the relevant times, relevant places. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Hermer out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I think we have no documents, although D108 which was not tendered before has been mentioned, but it is not tendered in evidence. That means that the Prosecution could call its next witness, but I think there are still a few remaining issues to deal with before. First of all, we have received the redacted Prosecution documents numbers 291305 and 315A, the redactions, just to consist of taking out parts that were not related to the evidence given by the witness. Is there any observation to be made in that respect from the side of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, I don't think there are any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Ierace, did I understand you well that you -- that you would give a short explanation on an issue which was dealt with by Mr. Stamp -- by -- yes, by Mr. Stamp, the issue of the medical records with, may I say what looks more or less as rubbed out entries. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have spoken to the relevant members of my team about that issue and it is, in my opinion, appropriate for there to be some enquiries made of the relevant people, the relevant institutions in Sarajevo. And we are tasking an investigator to make those enquiries. I expect that that will take at least a week. Therefore, any explanation that we will be in a position to provide to the Trial Chamber probably won't be before the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you will make further enquiries. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could Mr. Ierace remind us of the date when these documents were produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What document are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents, the medical documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I really don't understand what the purpose of that question is. And as my learned friend well remembers, it was Mr. Stamp who led that evidence. If he is anxious to know that date then I would be happy to provide it to him at the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Produced, the production of documents could mean different things, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When he wishes to tender to evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have to ask or do we know?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No when was that? I just wanted -- no, what I wanted is that Mr. Ierace could give us again the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...was approximately three weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is exactly what I remember, Mr. President, and therefore I believe it has been now for three weeks, and I think one would have had enough investigations to find out the exact date. Now the Defence would like to ask your Chamber if the Chamber can issue a decision whereby the -- telling us that these pieces, these documents, are not accepted because we cannot go on with this kind of suspense if they are going to be tendered in evidence or not, and it is never happening. So, as far as we are concerned, they should not be tendered. They cannot be tendered. One month notice is not acceptable, and the position of the Defence is such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...of course, we will consider your request. I have one additional question to you, Mr. Ierace. Is there any of the witnesses to be called in the very near future? That means, looking at my list, well, before the second part of next week, that would be in relation in whatever way with medical documents or -- the numbers are not enough for me to identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, we are talking about medical documents that are showing, well, call it multiple entries, call it manipulations. As the Defence prefers to say, call it "grattage." Of course, I would like to know exactly whether next week the Defence would be hindered in cross-examining the witnesses by not having an answer yet. Perhaps not all medical documents would cause the same problems. We have them of many different kinds. Could you please try to inform the Chamber after the next break on whether one of these specific documents that Mr. Piletta-Zanin is talking about would be introduced during the next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, Mr. President. When you say, "one of the documents, specific documents that Mr. Piletta-Zanin is talking about," do you mean documents that are affected by the signature of Dr. Dobraca, in other words, the entry that is troubling the Defence in relation to Dr. Dobraca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's in general terms. You can see on documents that there has been a previous entry at the same place. I think there have been already discussions of possible explanations like shortage of paper or whatever it might be. But that we know more about that and specifically asking whether one of these documents, where you can see that there had been something else before and there is now a new entry, whether one of these documents will be used during the next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will certainly make those enquiries, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber would like to know that before further considering the issue. That is of a totally different nature, but I would also like to deal with it before the weekend. General Galic, I was informed that your chair in the detention unit has been ordered but not yet arrived. I am just mentioning it in order to make clear to you that we try to pay proper attention to the matters raised before and that we will do that on a continuous basis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you very much. And I have to tell you that my medical condition, as far as the problems I had spoken to you before, has somewhat deteriorated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am sorry to hear that, that it has deteriorated. I have given instructions that the Chamber wants to be informed about every development in assisting you in overcoming the health problems. We know we are just human beings so we know it is not always possible, but whatever additional treatment might be necessary. So, therefore, I was just referring to the chair because that is one of the first and one of the most, I would say, one of the most simple issues to deal with. And the chair is coming, and of course we hope that it will -- we hope at least outbalance the deterioration and give some improvement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am trying to withstand this trial as much as I can, but you -- I would like to remind you of another suggestion of mine, to have a medical examination and to enable people who were in charge of my health for 30 years at the Belgrade military academy and to see what else can be done in order to help me go through this trial and perhaps later on, if need be, go and have a surgery. Well, this is very briefly what my request is all about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Galic, when I am talking about the chair, it is not that I think that would be the final solution, not at all. We have advised the -- your Defence to get in touch with those responsible and I have given instructions that whatever steps are made, whatever -- whatever developments are there, that the Chamber is informed about it. And of course, I take it that the Defence has also brought to the attention of those responsible your specific request for being examined by the doctors you would prefer to examine you. But the chair is a very easy thing and easy to be dealt with, and I was informed that it has been ordered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And I would like to tell you another thing that you are not aware of: The Defence has already put in a request with the head of the detention unit to have an appointment with him in order to discuss all of these ongoing problems. I am sorry if I have taken too much of your time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at all. We can't solve your problems, but we can keep a close eye that proper care is taken and we are, on a continuous basis, informed about the developments. I just wanted to let you know. As you know, whenever there is any specific health problem remaining for which you would like to ask the attention of the Chamber, we are always willing to listen to it and see what we can do about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would be any uncertainty about the transcript whether the documents P219, P305 or P315A, would have been admitted, I confirm that they were just a couple of minutes ago admitted into evidence. Is the Prosecution then ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I call Mr. Henneberry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, can you please escort Mr. Henneberry into the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, I would like to withdraw from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry - at least I assume that you are Mr. Henneberry - before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Henneberry. Mr. Henneberry, you will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is your full name Patrick Noel Henneberry?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you born on the 11th of April, 1960?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In 1979, did you join the armed forces of Canada?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you now retired from the Canadian Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: From the active forces, yes. I am still a member of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you retire from the active forces with the rank of Major?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In 1992, were you posted to UNPROFOR duties in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In that capacity, did you travel to Sarajevo on the 30th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you remain there until mid-February 1993?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you initially assume the position of senior military observer?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: On -- yes, on particular positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Ultimately, did you assume the position of commander on the north Lima side of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Lima being the side where observations were made of the equipment and activities of the Bosnian Serb army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you responsible for 32 UNMOs, being UNMO, United Nations Military Observers?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be shown a map which is Exhibit 742.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Ierace. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be possible for Mr. Ierace to have a map for General Galic. He would be able to look at it much better than I would or Ms. Pilipovic. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry, did this map come into your possession?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did it come into your possession during the course of your duties?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As you understand it, as of what date is the map accurate in terms of its depiction of various Lima positions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Fall of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In the bottom left-hand side of the map, there appears a black and white chart; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think that part of the map, Mr. President, would probably fit on the UNMO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace, you made the commitments as far as the -- could you please wait for one second, Mr. Usher. You made the commitments in respect of the UN confidential information. Do I understand that this is not to be regarded as protected, or at least this part of the map? I mean, we granted the protective measures but it was on the request of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is so, Mr. President. But that relates only to some of the documentary exhibits, not all of them

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
