utterances.text: We were not informed what documents were and what documents were not. And let's not discuss at this very moment whether it would have been appropriate to limit the protective measures to those documents that needed the protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you look at the letter that I think was copied to the Trial Chamber dated the 15th of May, that is yesterday, on the second page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have not perhaps read your mail of yesterday, but let me just have a look. Yes. I just received it. Yes, they are all, as far as I can see, 742 -- no 742 -- I see you made a distinction between those under Rule 70 and those not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, let's proceed. And would you please put on the ELMO, Mr. Usher, the chart at the left down corner of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Henneberry, the chart which is before you indicates across the top line "UNMO patrol base number." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And in the left-hand column going downwards, various types of weaponry. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On the face of it, the chart would appear to indicate the numbers of particular types of weaponry at various Lima positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Coming back to the top line, one sees that one of the columns is titled "Lima HQ." To what does that refer?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: That is the headquarters for the commander of the UNMOs based in Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. So am I correct in saying that the map indicates the various positions as of the fall of 1992 of certain Lima positions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: They being the ones, all of the ones that existed at that stage or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I couldn't say for sure. There is one other that I think was destroyed before this time. Let me rephrase, if I may. Yes, yes, to your answer, I do recall this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And again if we go to the black and white chart, in the bottom left-hand corner under "note 2," I think we see this stated: "These figures were taken from an undated document written in Sarajevo at some time between December and September of 1992." Do those words appear?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's put that to one side and come back to that later on. Now, as of mid-September 1992, whereabouts were you based?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I am sorry, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As of mid-September 1992, whereabouts were you based?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Specific position or -- I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Where did you sleep at nights?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I would have to look at my diary, because I moved occasionally from position to position. If I had a specific date, I could tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. But in a general sense, say between mid-September and the beginning of December, at what type of locations were you based?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I was at various Serbian positions, be they military establishments such as Lukavica, or other facilities that were held by the Serbians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At some point, did you become based at the Lukavica headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Permanently in December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Up until December, that is when you were permanently based there, did you visit the Lukavica headquarters and if so, how frequently?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I did visit. The frequency was dependent on the tactical situation, primarily. It ranged from once per week up to several times per week.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As part of your duties and the duties of other UNMOs, were documents known as Shoot-Reps prepared in which the number of outgoing and incoming shells or other projectiles were recorded?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you form any view as to how accurate these Shoot-Reps were?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: They were very inaccurate. Almost always, the count was lower than the actual number of rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How often were those documents prepared?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you identify what factors account for them being an underestimate of the actual number?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: There were three main reasons. First, we did not have a physical presence, "we" being the UNMO, at all of the known sites. And we knew there were other sites around Sarajevo that we were not permitted to enter. The second reason was that some of the UNMOs were not very diligent in their duties. And the third reason is frequently, I suppose, the number of rounds falling were so intense that it was not possible to distinguish from one to another or get an accurate count.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have told us that prior to sometime in December, you were based at places other than Lukavica headquarters. From time to time as part of your duties, did you make observations of gun positions on the Bosnian Serb army side of the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you form any view based on your observations as to the nature of the fire emanating from various gun positions that you observed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was that view?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Most of the indirect weapons, they being artillery or mortars, much of the time, they were fired indiscriminately without aiming and for no apparent reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think you still have in front of you the map which is Exhibit -- proposed Exhibit 742. Looking at that map, can you identify to us particular positions where you made those first-hand observations and formed that view?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Certainly. It might be easier to say that the only positions I didn't see firing from were Lima 12, Lima 13, and that would be all. The most intense firing that I observed came from the position monitored by Lima 7, Lima 3, Lima 11, and Lima 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. You have identified the observation posts from which you observed firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask for a clarification. The answer says that "the only position I didn't see firing from were Lima 1-2" - I understand it is Lima 12 - "and Lima 13 and that would be all." But then among the locations for the most intense firing I find Lima 12 again. Could you verify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I should have said Lima 2. I did not see firing from Lima 2 or Lima 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is clarifies the issue. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 8548 to 8550.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So you have identified to us the positions from which you observed firing. From which of those positions did you observe firing in circumstances where you formed the view that it was indiscriminate without aim and for no apparent reason?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Lima 3, Lima 10, Lima 11, Lima 12, Lima 7, and Lima 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, we are particularly interested in the period from, say, mid-September 1992. Did your last answer apply in all respects to the period after mid-September 1992 or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Let's go through some of those positions. Lima 7, what observations did you make from Lima 7 which led you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I observed numerous times soldiers firing weapons, indirect weapons, artillery and whatnot, without aiming, firing while they were intoxicated, moving some of the weapons by hand without aiming, firing what is called over open sites for an indirect weapon, which is not the proper procedure, and in discussions with the soldiers themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. I will ask you to explain some of the -- those observations you have related. When you say, "moving some of the weapons by hand without aiming," what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: If I may use an example of a mortar, for instance. It is a tube that points towards the sky and there should be a number of wheels and sights, optical sights with wheels, to which you move the barrel minutely by varying degrees. That is the only way a mortar can be fired accurately to the target it was intended, not a pinpoint target. I personally witnessed several times the soldiers moving it by hand or them by hand without checking their sights, without knowing where the round would land when fired, and in some cases, they actually just kicked the weapon. Whenever it stopped was fine, and they would fire that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to this fire you are telling us about, were you able to determine where the fire ended up? In other words, whether it ended up in the city of Sarajevo on the other sides of the confrontation lines or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: In many cases, yes, you could see the impact or I could see the impact in the city. There were several occasions where I did not see where the rounds landed, but on many occasions, yes, I could see them falling in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On any of those occasions where you did not actually see where those rounds landed, were you nevertheless able to arrive at a conclusion as to whether or not it would have landed somewhere in the city?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How far approximately was Lima 7 from the nearest point of the front line, just approximately?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Less than 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take it, therefore, that the city on the other side, as a matter of logic, was at its closest point something less than a kilometre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to mortars, perhaps a mortar directed at a target within the city, if you were to kick it or otherwise handle it in such a way that it moved, say, five degrees, what would that translate as in terms of distance in a target area? In other words, if it is moved a few degrees, is that a matter of a few metres in a target area or tens of metres or more or what?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Depending on the distance fired, it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to be extremely precise on these questions. I am sorry to interrupt, but the French transcript will not be exact. We are talking about five degrees and I would like to have the same thing in the French transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that proper care will be taken of you observation. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Taking you back to your earlier explanation as to your observations which led you to your view, you also said that you observed what is called "over open sites," firing over open sites for an indirect weapon. Could you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Similar to not using the optical sights to be precise on an indirect weapon, such as a mortar, artillery pieces use the same principal of a series of gears and sights fairly precise. On numerous occasions, I observed the soldiers simply looking with their naked eye down the barrel, moving it slightly, and firing that way, moving it by hand slightly without the use of the correct gears, and estimating where it would land, and firing the rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take you back to the question I asked you before my learned colleague rose to his feet, and I think you didn't have an opportunity to respond in full to that question. That is: If the mortar is moved, say, five degrees, what would that translate as in terms of distance in a target area? I think you said, "Depending on the distance fired, it would be," and that is as far as you got. Can you finish that answer, please?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It would be tens of metres, ranging to hundreds of metres, depending on the distance from in the case of a mortar, a baseplate, that being where the mortar is, to the impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Finally, in relation to the relevant observations which led to your formation of your view, you said that discussions with the soldiers themselves -- first of all, which soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Serbian soldiers on Lima 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What were those discussions, and I am asking you specifically about conversations which occurred after mid-September, 1992. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: The soldiers on Lima 7 and other positions, but Lima 7 as the example, told me frequently that they would just fire because they wanted to, at no particular target, on occasion. They were also or, rather, they also told me that sometimes they would fire in the case of another position just by the time of day in the general area of a target. And, again, with an indirect weapon, the method in which they moved them, it meant that there was no accuracy to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What do you think they meant by explaining that they were firing by the time of day in the general area of a target?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I have no doubt that they were using the fire as a psychological effect on the targets and the impact area, which included civilians and military.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you make any observations as to whether there was increased fire at particular times of day?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: On some positions, yes, there were. If I look at Lima 3 -- no, I am sorry, that is prior to September.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you make any observations from any observation post as to whether there were increased -- there was increased fire at particular times of day after mid-September 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes. Lima 10 and Lima 11 would open fire frequently around supper-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you work out any reason for that apparent pattern?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: It was to terrorise people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the rate of fire on those occasions? In other words, was it a matter of one or two shells or 10 shells or 20 shells in quick succession, or what? Please wait for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I apologise, but I have to say it, the French transcript says: "What was the right to fire?" I think they may have mistaken "rate" and "right."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that might be the case. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would there be any risk of confusion during this examination? I mean, if you would just write it down on a small yellow paper, because General Galic cannot be confused by it, Ms. Pilipovic cannot be confused by it. We are all listening to the original testimony. Mr. Ierace could not be confused by it. I do agree with you it is important to have a correct French transcript, but it is not necessary in order to achieve that to interrupt the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. President, but I am trying to do my best when I can. It is very hard to listen to and write at the same time. Thank you very much. I will do my very best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have to do that as well. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just before I repeat that question, Mr. Henneberry, I might make clear that all of my questions, unless otherwise indicated, refer to the period after mid-September 1992. What was the rate of fire on the occasions that you thought the objective was to terrorise people? Was it a matter of one or two shells or a larger number, or what?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: It depended on, I believe, just the whims of the soldiers and part of what I suspect was a battle plan. It could be as few as one round or as many as a number that couldn't be counted due to the rate of fire. Well over 10, 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So the situation, as I understand it, is that you were there as a United Nations military observer. Were you wearing any distinctive clothing to indicate your position?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I wore a blue beret or a blue helmet. I also wore a large Canadian flag, coloured flag, on my flack jacket which I wore most of the time, and on occasion, a bib. I don't know if that describes it. It is a pullover, a blue pullover that said "UN" on it, as well as a badge that identified me as a UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In any event, based firmly on your appearance, it was clear what your role was?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And in front of you, the gunning crews, the gun crews, rather, engaged in this form of fire, indiscriminate form of fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And admitted as much to you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you ever accompanied during these observations by any officers or liaison officers, in particular, from Lukavica, in other words, from the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I don't think. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever raise any of these concerns that you had, firstly, with the local commanders?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know what brigade the gun crews at Lima 7 came under?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On how many occasions, approximately, did you raise your concerns with the local commander, let's say, at Lima 7?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I can only say frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was that at Lima 7 itself or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: With the local commander, it was at Lima 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect his rank?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I believe he was a Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect his name?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, what did you say to him in relation to this indiscriminate fire directed at the city?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Many times, he would be asked to stop because it was indiscriminate. We frequently asked why there would be firing to a particular area and were often told that it was a matter of military tactics, and often we simply weren't given a reason or response.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: When you say, "We frequently asked why there would be firing to a particular area," did you say anything to make clear your concern as to the indiscriminate nature of the firing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes. Many times we would tell the local commander, not on Lima 7 but other positions, that the shells were falling inside the city where there was no opposing force, military presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You have told us that you did that frequently at Lima 7. On any of those occasions, did the local commander, the Lieutenant-Colonel, deny that it was happening?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you make complaints to the local commander at Lima 3?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On any occasion did that local commander deny that it was happening from Lima 3?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: The commander, I don't recall, but soldiers did deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say "soldiers," do you mean members of the gun crew or others?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, the members of the gun crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So you are saying that, if I understand you correctly, you formed the view they were firing indiscriminately, but they denied to you that they were on some occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, and there were times - I don't recall how many - when I was literally standing at the gun position while the guns were being fired - excuse me - and they declared that they weren't firing the guns. Excuse me for the smile, but I could see them being fired and they said, "We're not firing."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did they have smiles on their faces when they said that to you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Going back to the complaints that you made to the local commanders at Lima 3 and 7, you told us you don't recall if they ever denied it. Do you recall if they ever admitted it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. What is the state of your recollection as to their responses? I think you told us so far that they said something to the effect, or at least the one at Lima 7, said something to the effect that it was part of a military plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, on occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he ever attempt to explain how firing indiscriminately into a mixed urban area could be legitimately part of a military plan?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I can't say positively the commander at Lima 7, but several Serbian officers, commanders or officers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to ask Mr. Ierace to remind us exactly where we -- there is a mention of a military plan. I am sorry I am a little late but I am trying to be everywhere at the same time. Could Mr. Ierace give us the page and the line, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness -- if I could assist, Mr. Ierace, on page 57, line 14, the witness said, "Part of what I suspect was a battle plan." That is at least how he used the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, which page and which line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I said 57, line -- but let me just retrieve it. I think it is line 13 -- line 14: "What I suspect was a battle plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in fact, I have a different passage in mind. In the English transcript, it is page 59, the answer at line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 59, line 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we are talking about matter of military tactics. That is not exactly the same thing as military plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Which is why I used "words to the effect." I am happy to accommodated my learned colleague's concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Henneberry, saying to us earlier that when you protested the indiscriminate fire to the local commander at Lima 7, you said this: "Many times, he would be asked to stop because it was indiscriminate. We frequently asked why there would be firing to a particular area and were often told that it was a matter of military tactics, and often we simply weren't given a reason or response." Do you remember giving that answer earlier?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At Lima 3, were you ever given the same explanation, that it was a part of military tactics?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I was given that explanation on perhaps all positions and certainly most.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you make complaints to the local commanders at each of these positions where you observed fire and concluded that it was indiscriminate?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Did I make the complaint? I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you make complaints to the local commander at each of the Lima positions where you observed that behaviour?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And did any of them ever offer any other explanation that you could now recollect, other than "it was a matter of military tactics."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: They would elaborate occasionally on the military tactics they were speaking of. Lima 5, for instance, it was stated quite clearly that the tactic was to destroy the city and kill all of the Muslims inside. That was their statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when that was said to you, or was that more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: More than one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were any of those occasions after September 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes. All.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What were the ranks, the high ranks, of the individual who said that to you by way of explanation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Captains, majors, lieutenant-colonel, colonels.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you happen to know what brigade those officers were from?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take it you were given clearance by the Lukavica headquarters to attend and make observations from the various positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, you have told us about the complaints you made at the local level. Did you ever make any complaints to higher levels within the command structure of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was that to a particular individual or more than one individual?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: More than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: First of all, approximately how many individuals?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Five -- excuse me, five.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you take us through each of those five, who they were?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: There was a gentleman who claimed to be our liaison officer, who worked across the hall from my headquarters, my staff. There was an individual named Misha, who claimed at one point to be the operations officer. There was an individual named Indjic, sometimes called himself Indjic Miljenko, who was an intelligence officer on staff, and at least on one occasion, I made that same complaint to General Galic. There were also several, I would approximate 8 or 9 people, on the second floor of senior rank, and I don't recall their names or positions, to whom I made the same complaint or observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, first of all, which building are you referring to when you say, for instance, the second floor and the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I am talking about the Sarajevo Romanija Corps headquarters where I co-located my headquarters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just to be clear on it, whereabouts was that headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: In Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, were there a number of buildings at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was it a fairly large complex?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Where was this particular building in relation to -- within the complex in relation to the main entrance, that is the entrance closest to the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Right beside it. Metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many floors were there in this building?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I am going to say two, two above-ground floors. Frankly, I can't see the building in my mind right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, when you would find a suitable moment for the short break within the next couple of minutes, I would highly appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: This would be a convenient time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a short break. Our afternoon is a bit different from what it usually is. I would like to have a break of 17 minutes, so that makes 10 minutes past 6.00. Otherwise, there will only be 45 minutes left then we have 50 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 6.13 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise for being late, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I was asking you before the break about the headquarters. Where in the headquarters, if you know it, was the office of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: It was -- excuse me. It was on the second floor toward the centre of the building as I knew it. There were portions of the building that I did not get into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you and ask for a clarification. For in different countries and in different languages, ground floor, second floor. Sometimes the ground floor is the first floor. Would you please be clear on whether the second floor is two above the ground floor or is it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, second floor is two above ground floor. Actually, no. It is the second floor above the ground, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that has been clarified. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You would walk up the ground level one flight of stairs; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be given a sheet of paper and a pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry, can you draw on the piece of paper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could that be done on the ELMO, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially since it is not yet a classified document, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, I will ask you this question first: Was there a main entrance, if I could call it that, to the Lukavica complex?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did that main entrance come off -- I take it that main entrance came off a road?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Taking the top edge of the paper as north, could you first of all draw a line indicating the road in the area of the main entrance.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I will have the refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Also indicate the entrance in the road leading from it into the complex.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the ELMO operator can zoom it back.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I have identified, by way of two dots here, the headquarters, this being the road that was outside of the Lukavica compound; this being the main entrance here; this being the headquarters building itself, the first building as you came in to the -- generally, the south. This corner is where my headquarters, the UNMOs headquarters, was. And I would approximate from the part of the building that I recall or that I had access to, that General Galic's office would be just slightly left of the centre of the building on the second floor, with his windows facing generally south-west, sort of that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown the map which is Exhibit P3644.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am sorry, but since the witness has indicated many things in this -- this paper and on the screen, perhaps my learned colleague could give verbal indications for the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or if I could assist you. When the witness was mentioning a road outside the compound of Lukavica, he was referring to the vertical line, and left central entrance is where the horizontal line comes in to that line. The command building was the greatest rectangular. The part in the upper right-hand side, a very small rectangular black part, is where his office was and the arrows show the view from the offices of General Galic, and I see that the witness is now adding it all to the drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Henneberry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I ask that the witness be shown a copy of the standard Prosecution map which is Exhibit P3644. I have some blanks to provide to Your Honours and the Defence. And perhaps to save time, I think we are all reasonably familiar with it. We can open it at the folded section which depicts Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry, can you please open the map in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise, but I believe when the witness drew something which looked like a horizontal rectangle which was the main command building, he also drew a small black rectangle, and I do not see that this was mentioned, the smallest rectangle, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I clarify, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that you started writing already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was just an indication, that particular mark, an indication of slightly left of the centre of the building, and this particular mark here, if I divide the building like this, would be General Galic's office on the second -- on the floor above ground by one flight of stairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one stairs up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If it may assist for the benefit of the transcript, having regard to where you have placed north, you indicate General Galic's office to be on the southern side of the building. And going back to an earlier answer, there are two arrows on the diagram which indicate the direction of view that the General would have had through the window; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, would you please turn to the map that you have just been handed. Can you find on that map the complex of Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you see on that map the road which you have described in the diagram as "road outside of complex"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you also see on that map the road that comes off it at 90 degrees and alongside which is the headquarters building?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please take a blue pen and highlight the section of those two roads which appears in your diagram.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Do you also see in silhouette form the building which accommodated the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you draw with your blue pen an arrow ending at that particular silhouette?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That might be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry, I now take you back to the five individuals that you told us you complained to about indiscriminate fire into Sarajevo. The first of those you described as "a gentleman who claimed to be our liaison officer who worked across the hall from my headquarters, my staff." Do you know the name of that individual?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: No, sir, I am afraid I have forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect his rank?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect any distinctive features about his appearance?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: He was an elderly gentleman and, by that, I would put him seeming to appear in the mid-60 years of age range, perhaps slightly under.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was he ever uniformed when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was he always uniformed when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he have an office to himself or an office that he shared?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: It was sort of an open office concept with more than one person in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you complain to him on one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: More than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Approximately how many times?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I really couldn't even approximate, sir. It was several.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As to why you complained to him, you have told us that he claimed to be your liaison officer. Who did you understand be to represent in terms of liaison with you and the UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: The Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On how many occasions, approximately, did you complain to him after mid-September 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Several, perhaps less than 10, to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At any stage, did he suggest to you that you were mistaken in your conclusion that the fire was indiscriminate?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect what explanation, if any, he offered to you for it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he ever offer to take any action to stop it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: The action was that he would, like most of the people we complained to, that he would send our request forward, "forward" being up the chain of command, for consideration. And invariably -- most of the time, that statement was accompanied by a request for some form of action on the part of the United Nations or by the Muslim side. And it was clear that my request would not be accommodated unless his request for action was also accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you actually hand to him on any of those occasions a written complaint?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I couldn't say for sure that it was to him, sir. I did written complaints, but I couldn't say for sure it was to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying that, in effect, on some of those occasions, he said he would make a complaint further up the chain of his command?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And did he indicate whether his complaint would be in writing or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I don't believe so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On any occasion, did he report back to you on the results of a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, apologise. I know the transcripts are revised, but I can see the answer that the witness gave, the meaning, "I couldn't say for sure," and he also said that as far as he remembered, he wouldn't be able to say for certain which officer it was. But it is not just one word, it is a whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, you would agree with that and I think, as a matter of fact, that the witness testified that he does not remember whether it was specifically to this person that he handed over a written complaint. And that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps I will clarify it to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could clarify it to save time

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this is true, I think we have the missing part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that if just a whole part of a sentence falls away, then it might be more difficult to redact that, so I appreciate your assistance, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So on a number of occasions, you complained to a person you understood to be a senior officer and, what's more, a liaison officer within the SRK, of indiscriminate fire. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On any of those occasions -- shall I say following any of those occasions, did he report back to you on what action, if any, had been taken?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: First, if I may make a minor clarification. I don't believe I ever used the specific word "indiscriminate" fire. I would use a phrase such as, "the fire is landing on the UNMO position in the middle of town." I did not use the word "indiscriminate." And as far as getting back to me, I couldn't say for sure whether he did frequently. I could tell by getting on the radio whether the fire had ceased or not because I could contact one of my colleagues and they would tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On any of the occasions that you complained to him, did the fire cease shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I did?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. What did that indicate to you, if anything?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: That the consideration of my complaint was taken and an order had been called to ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember where the fire was originating from on any of those occasions that it stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and the witness just slow down a little for the interpreters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you able to say, although you don't recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the message passed, I believe the message on the slowing down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was. You hear it in French, we hear it in English. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Although you don't recall the specific places of origin, does your memory serve you sufficiently to say whether those sources were Lima observations post positions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: The sources of the fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Or sites monitored by the Lima observation positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, the second person that you mentioned you complained to, I think you said there was an individual named Misha someone who claimed at one point to be the operations officer. The transcript hasn't at this stage recorded the name that you gave. Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: The name he used was Misha, "M" as in "Michael" i-s-h-a, and he claimed to be the corps operations officer. And I say "claimed." I don't personally believe he was the senior operations officer, just by way of his age and location in the building. But he was -- he was involved with operations, and perhaps his understanding of what an operations officer is and mine differed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On how many occasions after September 1992 did you personally complain to him in terms similar to your complaint to the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: To him, it was few. I would say less than five.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was his response on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Indifference, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he ever offer any action or further report up his chain of command?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I don't recall whether he did or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If you recollect, what was it about him, either his appearance or what he said, that led you to conclude that his response to your concerns was one of indifference?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Body language, shrugging, no verbal response, ignored my complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you speak to him through the services of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I believe he spoke English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Incidently, the first person you mentioned, did you communicate with him through an interpreter or in English?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Through an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect Misha's rank?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he wear a uniform when you typically saw him?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, but his uniform was a different colour than the standard green camouflage of soldiers. His was a solid blue. Similar, but not quite a police uniform. Similar to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever see any room in the headquarters which seemed to be an operations room?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: An operations planning room, yes. An operations centre, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did this gentleman, Misha, seem to have an office somewhere in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whereabouts was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. The third person that you mentioned was an individual named Indjic, who you described as an intelligence officer on staff, although I may have confused two individuals in that description. Did you mean by "intelligence officer" the person named Indjic or another person?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he seem to have an office in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: He had an office directly across from the entrance to the UNMO site.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was that a shared office or an office just for him?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I believe it was his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know what rank he was at that stage?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: When I started, he claimed to be a captain, and at some time in the winter, he was promoted to major.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he always wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: The vast majority of the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he ever say to you what his job was?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes. He said he was the, not "a," but "the" intelligence officer for the corps. I did not believe him in that, but I did believe that he was a trained intelligence officer. By that, I mean trained in the skill and art of intelligence collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say that you did not believe his claim to be the intelligence officer for the corps, did you form any view as to what his job, in fact, was?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: His job was in part to try to get intelligence from the UNMOs. Of that, there is no doubt. He also had, and spoke to me on several occasions, of intelligence that he personally gathered or was given on the status of the Muslim forces. Finally, he knew frequently, and perhaps always, of the larger-scale plans of the corps, and by that I mean the corps plan, the brigade plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in the company of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On how many occasions after September 1992 did you complain to him about shelling of Sarajevo in particular, shelling of civilian areas?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Dozens and dozens, if not hundreds. I met with him daily, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before you moved into the Lukavica headquarters, that is before that time whenever it was in December 1992, how many times per week would you complain to him about such shellings?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: To him, less than once a week before I moved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you moved in, then how often?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Dozens upon dozens, if not hundreds. There would be days when I would spend six hours with him. There were days whether I would meet with him 20 or 30 times. There were other days when we didn't meet or the contact was less frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What can you tell us as to his response, typically, if there was a typical response, to your complaints about civilians in the city being shelled?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Initially, there was much rhetoric about why the Serbs were shelling the Muslims civilians and military, how the Serbs had been persecuted over the centuries. As we got to know each other and in fact developed a rapport, he had admitted to me that he knew civilians were being shelled and were dying and that he believed it was wrong, but it simply was going to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he explain to you why he thought it was going to continue?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes. The ultimate goal, as explained by Indjic and indeed General Mladic himself, was to either destroy the city or rid it of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You said just then and I am quoting from the transcript, " and indeed General Mladic himself."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So coming back to Indjic, he told you that he believed it was wrong, but it simply was going to continue, and he explained to you why he thought it was going to continue, namely, because the ultimate goal was to either destroy the city or rid it of Muslims. Have I accurately reflected back to you your evidence so far?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he say anything as to where the orders were coming from to that end?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Other than an indication - perhaps not a direct statement per se - but an indication that it was the corps plan. Specifically from who, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was that in a particular conversation or a series of conversations that you had with him that he indicated, to use your word, that it was the corps plan?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Several conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you remember at this stage -- well, first of all, did you speak to him in English or a different language?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you remember the words that he used or any of the words that he used which indicated to you that he was communicating that it was the corps plan? And take your time to think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be precise and since the witness is going to take his time, would it be possible for Mr. Ierace to be more precise about which army corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will take that on board, Mr. President, and I will come back to that

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think it is perfectly clear from the line of questioning, but if I do -- yes, please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the words he used that indicated to you that it was the corps plan?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Not particularly no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. When he spoke of the corps in these various conversations that you had with him, which particular corps were you and he discussing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: The Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you at any stage about the way in which that corps plan, as you understood it, was communicated down to the, for instance, level of the gun crews?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic did not tell me but I saw other ways or witnessed the ways in which the information would flow from the corps headquarters right down to individual soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what they were, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes. Occasionally, and I simply -- I couldn't say how many times, the senior officers who were on brigade staff, or perhaps brigade commanders, would come to the headquarters. Radio transmissions were also used at least at the brigade headquarters level, presumably up and down, and from that, I saw, getting down into the brigade and perhaps lower unit status, down to the soldier level, the orders were usually transmitted verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How did you know it was the brigade commanders who would come to the headquarters? Was it a matter of you recognising them or some other means?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: On a few occasions, I recognised individuals who said they were brigade commanders. Generally, it was the way in which they arrived and what they were doing that made me believe they were brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was that method of arrival?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: They would have a driver and a vehicle. They would get out and be escorted with some deference to their status and they would go upstairs if they were senior.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say "go upstairs," what was there upstairs, apart from the office of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: The operations planning room that I discussed earlier was up there. There were telephone communications as a minimum, perhaps others. There were some accommodations. There were restricted areas that I simply didn't get into.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know whether those restricted areas were staffed? In other words, whether there were offices there or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In those conversations, in those long and repeated conversations with Major Indjic, did he express any misgivings about the campaign, apart from acknowledging that it was wrong? I should say by "campaign," I mean the shelling of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: No, other than he did not give or transmit to me any misgivings other than on occasion, towards the end, he stated that the shelling of the civilians was wrong, in his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Apart from whether or not he communicated any misgivings to you, did he indicate any unwillingness on his part to stay in his position, whatever that position was?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Just the opposite, sir. He indicated that he intended to stay and was looking forward to senior appointments and promotion within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: One might hear those words and conclude that although he knew it was wrong, he was untroubled by it and embraced it. Were you able to conclude from your observations what his attitude to it was, even though he knew it was wrong? And of course I am talking about the deliberate shelling of civilian areas of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two remarks. This question is in relation to a simple psychological consideration of a person and I don't think that we could answer such -- anyone could answer such a question. And the second remark is that I have a lot of difficulties following. I would like to ask for everyone to slow down because I have to write these corrections for the French booth. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I do press the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I do press the question, meaning that I understand my learned colleague objects to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, he said he made some remarks, but I think he is complaining since you are asking about the judgment of the witness of someone else's mind, if I am...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Except that the key words in my question were, "Were you able to conclude from your observations." I am happy to turn the question around if you wish it, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to have it more in a factual way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You told us that you spent many hours with him, sometimes, I think you said six hours on one occasion; that you complained to him hundreds of times in the period that you were in Lukavica headquarters, complained to him hundreds of times about the shelling of civilian areas in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And he was sufficiently candid with you on a number of those occasions -- withdraw that. He was sufficiently candid with you on a number of occasions that he believed it to be wrong. That's your evidence, I think?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He also conveyed to you enthusiasm in remaining in his job, although he had indicated to you that he believed it was wrong?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you make any observations about him when he --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really sorry, Mr. President, but now the French booth is putting in the text he said that "this campaign was not correct." Now, Mr. Ierace did not precisely use the word "campaign," and we know why, and now it is going to be in the French transcript. This is something entirely new and I have to intervene now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you please indicate exactly on what line this happened because I am not following the French?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Earlier -- I am following both interpretations. Earlier, Mr. Ierace was just -- [In English] Line 11, page 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you please -- it might also have been caused by the speed, of course, and that is two people speaking the same language. That is what often happens. Could you please resume at line -- page 83, line 11, or just before, and repeat your question so that it will be properly translated. I do respect that Mr. Piletta-Zanin listens to the text in his own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Line 11 in the English transcript is halfway through a sentence, so perhaps from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invited you a few lines before so that at least line 11 is included.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry, you told us that you spent many hours with Major Indjic, on at least one occasion, six hours. You have also told us that you complained to him hundreds of times during the period that you were at Lukavica headquarters about the shelling of civilian areas in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He was sufficiently candid with you to tell you that he knew the shelling of the civilians in Sarajevo to be wrong; is that also your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, he conveyed to you enthusiasm in remaining in his job; is that so?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Remaining and progressing to higher levels of rank, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, that enthusiasm, was that expressed in one conversation or a number of conversations?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Several conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was it at a particular period of time, as you remember it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: It would likely have been January on, after Indjic and I developed a rapport that allowed us to be candid.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How did that enthusiasm express itself to you? Was it in the tone of his voice, the words he used, his body language or what?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Generally, the phrase that he was looking forward to a long career promotion. The tone of his voice conveyed enthusiasm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was there anything about those factors, the words he used, the tone, or his body language, which indicated to you comfort with that activity of the deliberate shelling of civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes. In the sense that although he personally disagreed with it, he believed that it was a necessity of doing and conducting military business. He did not say that specifically, but his attitude, I suppose, showed that he was not discomfort -- not terribly upset about it. It was the corps plan and it was a necessary [Real-time transcript read in error "unnecessary"] evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, going back to the earlier period of your acquaintance with him, in those earlier days when you complained about the shelling of civilians in Sarajevo, did he, in those days, ever deny that it was happening?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he ever suggest to you that you or your observers were mistaken in what they saw?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he ever say that if it happened, it was uncontrollable element?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And yet later, once he fell into your confidence, your evidence is that he not only admitted that it happened, but that it was wrong?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In other words, your evidence is, as I understand it, and please correct me if I am wrong, he ceased to deny it, admitted it and said it was wrong, but necessary?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next area of my examination-in-chief will concern General Galic and the remaining individual that the witness has identified as a senior officer to whom he complained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it would be inappropriate to start dealing with that in two minutes. May I just, therefore, take it, of your last answer to the question of Mr. Ierace that where the transcript says that it was the Corps's plan and it was an "unnecessary evil," that you said it was a necessary evil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Necessary. It was required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is line 1 on page 86.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we adjourn, you asked me to enquire and I have done that. And in relation to the witnesses to be called, there is one witness where there are medical records on the exhibit list, and that is Husovic. We have checked the quality of the documents and the original is a very poor copy. That is not to say that there are signs on it of changes being made, but simply it is poor quality copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have noticed that it is certain types of documents where it is repeatedly found. I think it takes not more than five minutes to see whether this would hinder the Defence in a specific way by cross-examining that witness, so that and if true, then we will be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It does not have to be done necessarily today, but we would need some time on next Tuesday for the evidence of the present witness. That means that we will -- since we are not sitting tomorrow, since we are not sitting on Monday, that we will adjourn until next Tuesday at 9.00, in the morning same courtroom, and please, Mr. -- Mr. Henneberry, would you be then again be present in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it - I never indicated this before - but I take it that there will be no further talks with the Prosecution while during the next weekend, that is for you. That is so that there will be no further discussions on your testimony, and especially it is a long weekend. But that you will be here again on Tuesday morning and we then will resume the examination-in-chief, and later on, you will be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until next Tuesday, 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 7.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of May, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
